sources.title: Plantains: identification and management
sources.supportingPassageParaphrased: Narrowleaf (buckhorn) plantain: clump-forming rosette with a short thick caudex; tiny white flowers in a cylindrical or cone-shaped cluster on a slender leafless stalk under 1 ft; leaves lanceolate, much longer than wide, with 3-5 prominent nearly parallel veins, entire or subtly toothed margins; common plantain (P. major) has oval leaves; blackseed plantain (P. rugelii) differs in bract shape and capsule splitting.

sources.title: Assessment report on Plantago lanceolata L., folium (22 Nov 2011)
sources.supportingPassageParaphrased: Herbal substance contains about 2-3% iridoid glycosides (aucubin and catalpol main), mucilage polysaccharides, flavonoids (apigenin, luteolin), phenylethanoids (acteoside, plantamajoside), phenol carboxylic acids and tannins; records traditional indications (catarrh of the respiratory tract, inflammation of mouth/throat mucosa, external use on inflamed skin; folk use on wounds); states controlled clinical studies supporting a well-established use have not been performed while traditional use is well documented; anti-inflammatory activity of single constituents shown in vitro and in animals.

sources.title: Ethnobotanical uses, chemical constituents and application of Plantago lanceolata L.
sources.supportingPassageParaphrased: Review of folk uses: leaf as emollient, demulcent, expectorant; leaf powder or heated leaves applied to wounds and swellings; use for insect and snake bites reported in Turkey; lists aucubin and catalpol as main iridoid glycosides and acteoside as a main phenylethanoid; wound-healing effects described in rodent studies.

sources.title: Plantago mechanisms for enhanced wound healing: a review on bioactive phytoconstituents
sources.supportingPassageParaphrased: P. lanceolata is traditionally used for wound therapy in Pakistan and Iraq and has been tested in vivo (animal) for wound healing and anti-inflammatory effects.

sources.publisher: Phytopharmacy: An Evidence-Based Guide to Herbal Medicinal Products (Wiley), chapter by Beara
sources.title: Ribwort plantain chapter summary
sources.supportingPassageParaphrased: Summary: main constituents are iridoid glycosides, mucilage, flavonoids, phenylethanoids; used mainly for upper respiratory tract inflammation and as a demulcent for dry cough, and topically for inflammatory skin conditions; fresh leaves used in Scotland as a poultice or ointment on fresh wounds.

sources.title: Plantago uses, benefits and dosage
sources.supportingPassageParaphrased: A monograph covering several Plantago species (including P. lanceolata, P. major and the psyllium species). Psyllium seed husk with insufficient fluid can swell and block throat/oesophagus; the FDA label warning is quoted; Plantago pollen contains allergens; psyllium seed allergy including anaphylaxis reported.
sources.caveat: Its swelling and obstruction evidence concerns psyllium products (P. ovata / P. psyllium / P. afra), not P. lanceolata.

sources.title: Community herbal monograph on Plantago afra L. et Plantago indica L., semen
sources.supportingPassageParaphrased: For psyllium seed (P. afra and P. indica): must be taken with sufficient liquid; with inadequate fluid bulk-forming agents can obstruct the throat and oesophagus with choking; seeds contain potent allergens; absorbs up to ten times its weight in water.
sources.caveat: Applies to P. afra/P. indica, NOT to P. lanceolata.

sources.title: Foraging guide: ribwort plantain
sources.supportingPassageParaphrased: Says leaves are bright green, narrow, with 3-5 raised ribs beneath, stem deeply grooved; confusable with hoary plantain and greater plantain (both much wider leaves, neither poisonous); unopened flower heads eaten raw taste mushroom-like, leaves edible but bitter; 'hazards none known'.
sources.caveat: LOW authority: a business page, no citations. Used only where nothing better was found, and every such use is flagged.

sources.title: Plantain materia medica
sources.supportingPassageParaphrased: Says there are no known toxic lookalikes for any Plantago species and compares narrowleaf plantain to yellow/curly dock.
sources.caveat: LOW authority; no citations; used only to note that dock is raised as a lookalike.

lookalikes.name: Plantago major (broadleaf plantain; existing card #14)
lookalikes.how_to_tell: Oval leaves with 3-5 parallel veins, wavy edges on older leaves, cylindrical leafless spike.
lookalikes.note: Not dangerous: no hazard difference found. Both are separate cards.

lookalikes.name: Plantago rugelii (blackseed plantain)
lookalikes.how_to_tell: Similar to P. major; differs in bract shape and how capsules split (magnification may be needed).

lookalikes.name: Plantago media (hoary plantain)
lookalikes.how_to_tell: Much wider leaves than P. lanceolata (low-authority source).

lookalikes.name: Rumex crispus (curly dock rosette) - proposed card #67
lookalikes.how_to_tell: NOT FOUND from an authoritative source (the herbalist site only says to compare).
lookalikes.note: Both are cards in this pilot; a rosette confusion between them would be card-level.

lookalikes.name: Any toxic plant
lookalikes.how_to_tell: Two low-authority pages say no toxic lookalike is known; NO authoritative source on this was found. Not evidence of absence.

safety.question: What cautions apply to narrowleaf plantain, and does 'Seeds swell; drink plenty of water' apply to this species?

whatSourcesSay.summary: The EMA assessment report on the leaf (read in excerpt) recorded traditional use and constituents; no hazard statement for the leaf was found in the excerpt read.

whatSourcesSay.position: Seed swelling / obstruction applies to psyllium
whatSourcesSay.summary: Swelling and throat-obstruction warnings are documented for psyllium seed (P. afra/P. indica/P. ovata) products. NOT FOUND for P. lanceolata seed or husk.
Plantago pollen contains allergens and psyllium has caused anaphylaxis; the genus-level pollen statement is not specific to this species.

safety.whereTheyDisagree: No disagreement; a gap. The draft's seed-swelling caution is borrowed from psyllium and is not sourced for P. lanceolata.

draftCardWarningReview.cardWarning: Seeds swell; drink plenty of water.
draftCardWarningReview.verdict: UNSUPPORTED AS WRITTEN for this species (NOT FOUND for P. lanceolata). It is a sound caution for psyllium products, and the card lists 'Seed Fiber' as a preparation and 'Seed' as a usable part, neither of which is sourced for P. lanceolata. As written it also reads as preparation advice (how to take seeds safely).

safety.proposedSiteCaution: PROPOSED DRAFT FOR REVIEW, NOT FINAL WORDING: 'Seeds of some plantain species (psyllium) swell in liquid and can block the throat if swallowed without plenty of water. This has not been studied for narrowleaf plantain. Plantdex does not recommend eating the seeds or any wild plant.' Alternative: drop the seed lines from this card until they are sourced.
openSafetyQuestions: Remove 'Seed Fiber' and 'Seed' from the draft, or source them for P. lanceolata?
Does the owner want an allergy line (pollen)? Genus-level only.
Is 'Bite soothing' appropriate even as a traditional-use phrase when snake bites are mentioned in the source? Recommend rewording or omitting.

reviewOfDraft.note: Folk use on wounds is well documented per the EMA report; the EMA also says controlled clinical studies have not been performed. Animal studies exist (PRECLINICAL).
A Turkish folk record covers insect and snake bites. Reword or omit; do not imply treatment of any bite.
Traditional use for respiratory-tract catarrh and dry cough is recorded; no efficacy claim should be rendered.
PRECLINICAL: in vitro and animal anti-inflammatory activity of constituents (acteoside, aucubin, catalpol). Not a human finding; do not render as a trait.
Main iridoid glycoside; content varies with leaf age (young leaves higher in catalpol, older in aucubin per EMA).
A named phenylethanoid (also called verbascoside in the literature).
Only a low-authority page says leaves are bitter. NOT FOUND from a reputable source.
Only a low-authority page. NOT FOUND from a reputable source.
Fresh or heated leaves applied to wounds is a documented folk practice.
NOT FOUND for P. lanceolata; documented for psyllium species only.
The leaf (folium) is the herbal substance in the EMA assessment.
Unopened flower heads eaten per a low-authority page only.
'Wound' as traditional topical use; 'edible' not sourced beyond a low-authority page.

scannerAndMatchingNotes: P. major is card #14 and P. lanceolata a different exact species: exact-only matching sends each to its own card; genus-wide matching would not. A hybrid between them is not described in the sources read (NOT FOUND).
